notes:
Below is a verse‑by‑verse commentary on Jeremiah 29, drawing on the sources I was able to read. Each point is followed by its source URL.

---

## vv. 1–3: Historical Setting and Delivery of the Letter

**v. 1 – “This is the text of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem…”**
- The chapter opens a letter from Jeremiah to the exiles already in Babylon after the 597 BC deportation under Jeconiah. Although a written letter, it carries full prophetic authority as God’s word.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-29-commentary

- Gill notes the letter was addressed to the “residue of the elders” – some leaders had already died en route or shortly after arrival.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

- Ellicott observes that the spelling “Jeremiah” (rather than the usual “Jeremiahu”) in the Hebrew may indicate that the opening verse was added by a later hand.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

**v. 2 – “(This was after King Jeconiah… had been exiled from Jerusalem.)”**
- This parenthetical remark anchors the letter after the second deportation (597 BC). Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) reigned only three months before being taken. The “queen” is the queen-mother Nehushta (2 Kings 24:8).  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-29-commentary  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

- The removal of craftsmen and smiths was a deliberate Babylonian strategy: it stripped Judah of skilled workers while providing labour for Nebuchadnezzar’s building projects.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-29-commentary

**v. 3 – “The letter was entrusted to Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah…”**
- The two messengers came from families associated with Josiah’s reforms. Elasah was probably the brother of Ahikam, who had protected Jeremiah (Jer 26:24). Gemariah was likely the son (or grandson) of Hilkiah the high priest who found the Book of the Law (2 Kings 22:4–8).  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-29-commentary  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

- Zedekiah sent these men on a diplomatic mission to Babylon (perhaps paying tribute), and Jeremiah’s letter was carried alongside royal correspondence. It is uncertain whether Zedekiah knew the contents.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-29-commentary

---

## v. 4: God Is the True Author of the Exile

**v. 4 – “This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says to all the exiles…”**
- The crucial phrase is “whom **I** have sent into exile.” Though Nebuchadnezzar was the human agent, God declares Himself the ultimate cause of the deportation. This is meant to reorient the exiles’ thinking: they are not merely victims of geopolitics but under God’s sovereign discipline.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-29-commentary  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

- Gill observes that the divine titles “LORD of hosts” and “God of Israel” were chosen to remind the exiles that the God who commands all armies remains their covenant God, even in a pagan land.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

---

## vv. 5–7: Settle Down, Seek the City’s Peace

**v. 5 – “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce.”**
- This command directly contradicted the message of the false prophets, who promised a quick return. God told the exiles to settle in for the long haul. Guzik cites Cundall: “Most likely, in expectation of a brief sojourn in captivity, they were wary of acquiring houses, land, and even children.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

- Feinberg notes that the freedom to build, plant, and own property “implies they were neither slaves nor prisoners in their new land.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**v. 6 – “Take wives… Multiply there; do not decrease.”**
- God wanted the exilic community to grow, not shrink — just as Israel had multiplied in Egypt. The instructions cover multiple generations (take wives for your sons, give your daughters in marriage), indicating an exile lasting at least two generations.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

- Gill specifies that they were not to intermarry with pagan Chaldeans but with fellow Jews, since marriage to heathens was forbidden.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

**v. 7 – “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf…”**
- This command was, as Feinberg notes, “unique in ancient literature.” To pray for pagan captors was almost unthinkable. Ellicott calls it “the hardest command of all” — it required superhuman patience not to curse Babylon.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

- The Hebrew word for “peace/prosperity” is *shalom*. Ryken (cited by Guzik) notes that prayer and good works are ways to seek *shalom*, but “by themselves, random acts of kindness cannot bring enduring peace. The only basis for real and lasting shalom is the work of Jesus Christ on the cross.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

- Ellicott draws a parallel to 1 Timothy 2:2, where Christians under Nero were told to pray for the emperor.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

---

## vv. 8–9: Warning against False Prophets

**v. 8 – “Do not be deceived by the prophets and diviners among you…”**
- False prophets in Babylon (just as in Jerusalem) were promising a speedy end to exile. The unusual phrase “dreams you elicit from them” suggests the people were actively soliciting comforting visions.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

- Thompson (cited by Guzik) notes there was a period of unrest across the Babylonian empire around 595/4 BC, and prophets in both Jerusalem and Babylon were proclaiming Babylon’s imminent collapse.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**v. 9 – “For they are falsely prophesying to you in My name; I have not sent them…”**
- Gill emphasises: these prophets had no commission or authority; they “ran without being sent.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

---

## vv. 10–14: The Promise of Restoration

**v. 10 – “When Babylon’s seventy years are complete, I will attend to you…”**
- Jeremiah had previously announced the seventy-year exile (Jeremiah 25:11–12). Here he reaffirms it. Spurgeon is quoted (by Guzik): “The prophet had the double duty of putting down their false hopes, and sustaining their right expectations.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

- R.K. Harrison counts the seventy years from the Babylonian victory at Carchemish (605 BC) to the first return of exiles (536 BC).  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

- The word “completed” indicates that the seventy years fulfills God’s appointed time of discipline — not a year sooner or later.  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-29-commentary

**v. 11 – “For I know the plans I have for you… plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.”**
- Ellicott gives the most precise rendering: the Hebrew literally means “to give you **a future and a hope**” (not “an expected end”). “The ‘future’ tells them that their history as a people is not yet over; the ‘hope’ that there is a better time in store for them.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

- Feinberg notes that the phrase is a hendiadys: “a hopeful end.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

- Gill expands theologically: God’s “thoughts of peace” ultimately point to the Messiah, “in whom all God’s thoughts of peace, concerning his special people, issue.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

- Guzik stresses that these were God’s thoughts toward Israel under the Old Covenant; we should not dare believe He is less favourable to New Covenant believers. He adds: “It is the devil’s deception to rob God’s people of their sense of His future and a hope for them.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**vv. 12–13 – “Then you will call upon Me… You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.”**
- Ellicott hears in these words “the infinite tenderness” of God and sees them as an anticipation of Christ’s words in Matthew 7:8: “He that seeketh findeth.” The language echoes Deuteronomy 4:29–30.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

- Even in exile, without the temple and its rituals, God would listen when His people prayed. Their prayer would be part of their “future and hope.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**v. 14 – “I will restore you from captivity and gather you from all the nations…”**
- The language broadens beyond Babylon to “all the nations,” suggesting a wider, perhaps eschatological gathering. Gill sees this as referring to the fuller return under Cyrus and beyond.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

---

## vv. 15–20: Judgment on Those Who Remained in Jerusalem

**v. 15 – “Because you may say, ‘The LORD has raised up for us prophets in Babylon,’”**
- Some exiles boasted that they had their own prophets in Babylon and did not need Jeremiah. These false prophets were telling them what they wanted to hear.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

**vv. 16–17 – “I will send against them sword and famine and plague, and I will make them like rotten figs…”**
- God turns to address the fate of those still in Jerusalem under Zedekiah. The “rotten figs” image is drawn from Jeremiah 24. Clarke (cited by Guzik) says: “Do not envy the state of Zedekiah who sits on the throne of David, nor that of the people who are now in the land whence ye have been carried captive.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**vv. 18–19 – “I will make them a horror… because they have not listened to My words…”**
- The language of curse, desolation, scorn, and reproach describes the fate of those who repeatedly rejected God’s word through His prophets. Guzik notes that God’s objection was against the sense of superiority held by those who remained.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**v. 20 – “So hear the word of the LORD, all you exiles I have sent away…”**
- A fresh summons to the exiles to heed God’s true word rather than the lies of false prophets.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

---

## vv. 21–23: Judgment on the False Prophets Ahab and Zedekiah

**v. 21 – “About Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah…”**
- These two false prophets are otherwise unknown. Ellicott notes they were likely leaders of the party of revolt in Babylon, prophesying Nebuchadnezzar’s imminent downfall.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

- Their names are ironically those of a wicked king of Israel and a wicked king of Judah.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**v. 22 – “May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire!”**
- Their execution by burning became a proverbial curse among the exiles. Ryken (cited by Guzik) notes this was “the proper punishment for treason in Hammurabi’s Code.” Ellicott observes that the name Kolaiah (possibly derived from a verb meaning “roasting”) may have made the punishment a grim wordplay.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

**v. 23 – “For they have committed an outrage… adultery… speaking lies in My name…”**
- Besides false prophecy, these men were guilty of adultery. Ellicott suggests they may have thought that Jehovah, being the God of Israel, did not exercise His power in distant Babylon — but God declares, “I am He who knows, and I am a witness.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

---

## vv. 24–28: Shemaiah’s Letter against Jeremiah

**v. 24 – “You are to tell Shemaiah the Nehelamite…”**
- Shemaiah was a false prophet in Babylon who reacted against Jeremiah’s letter. The name “Nehelamite” may be a wordplay on the Hebrew *halam* (“dreamer”).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

**vv. 25–26 – “You said to Zephaniah: ‘The LORD has appointed you priest in place of Jehoiada…’”**
- Shemaiah wrote to the priest Zephaniah in Jerusalem, demanding that he silence Jeremiah. Jehoiada (the previous chief officer) had apparently been deposed for not supporting the revolt party’s hard line.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm

- Clarke notes that the word translated “madman” is *meshugga* — a term of scorn used for those in ecstatic prophetic states (cf. 2 Kings 9:11; Hosea 9:7).  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**vv. 27–28 – “Why have you not rebuked Jeremiah…? For he has sent to us in Babylon, claiming: Since the exile will be lengthy…”**
- Shemaiah’s complaint confirms that Jeremiah’s message — settle down, build houses, plant gardens — had reached Babylon and was being taken seriously. Ellicott notes some render the Hebrew of v.28 as “It is far off,” implying Jeremiah thought distance gave him immunity.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

---

## vv. 29–32: Zephaniah’s Response and God’s Judgment on Shemaiah

**v. 29 – “(Zephaniah the priest, however, had read this letter to Jeremiah the prophet.)”**
- Zephaniah did not comply with Shemaiah’s demand. Instead, he read the letter to Jeremiah — possibly to warn him, or perhaps to pressure him. Ellicott compares this to the Pharisees who reported Herod’s threats to Jesus (Luke 13:31).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/29.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

**vv. 30–32 – “I will surely punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants…”**
- God’s judgment on Shemaiah is severe: his line will die out, and he will not “see the good that I will bring to My people.” The ultimate charge is that “he has preached rebellion against the LORD.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/29.htm

- Guzik draws the application: “One reason to keep faithful to God through the difficulties of life is simply so we can be around when God does remarkable good for His people.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-29/

## Traditions and Distinctive Readings

### Reformed / Conservative Evangelical (on v. 11)

- Ligonier (Sproul’s ministry) teaches that Jeremiah 29:11 is “one of the most misapplied verses in all of Scripture.” Some take it to mean God promises earthly prosperity and a trouble‑free life; that is a distortion. The original promise was to exiles under judgment.  
  https://www.ligonier.org/posts/jeremiah-2911 (from search excerpts)

- John Piper (Desiring God) argues that Christians **can** legitimately claim this promise — but only because of Christ. At the Last Supper, Jesus inaugurated the New Covenant in His blood, securing all covenant promises for His people. 2 Corinthians 1:20 says “all the promises of God find their Yes in Him.” So a Gentile believer may embrace Jeremiah 29:11 as a promise purchased by Christ, though the immediate historical fulfilment belonged to Israel.  
  https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/is-jeremiah-29-11-a-promise-to-christians

- The Gospel Coalition similarly affirms that “if you are in Christ, you can count on it” — but it does not promise the kind of future American culture prizes; short‑term, one may suffer. Long‑term, one’s future is co‑signed with Christ.  
  https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/jeremiah-2911-apply/

### Baptist / MacArthur (GTY)

- John MacArthur’s ministry (GTY) strongly criticises prosperity preachers (Osteen, Stanley, Warren) for ripping Jeremiah 29:11 from its context. In context, God gave the promise while His foot was on Israel’s neck in judgment. Those who received the promise would likely not live to see its fulfilment 70 years later. The true lesson is God’s covenant faithfulness — He does not abandon His people even in deserved exile.  
  https://www.gty.org/blogs/B150925/did-god-promise-you-prosperity

### Prosperity / Word of Faith Misuse

- Prosperity teachers commonly cite Jeremiah 29:11 as a guarantee of health, wealth, and earthly success for believers. Desiring God identifies this as one of several hermeneutical errors: taking verses out of context, naively literal reading of figurative language, an over‑realised eschatology, and misapplication. The prosperity gospel “redefines blessing as guaranteed wealth, obscuring the cross‑bearing call of discipleship.”  
  https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-gods-of-the-prosperity-gospel  
  https://biblehub.com/q/Is_Jeremiah_29_11_a_promise_of_prosperity.htm
